opening.headline: Determine whether you want to create the latest information retrieval and code execution functionality yourself or use a provided tool based on the change burden.
body: Let's say your in-house question-and-answer app starts fielding questions about things like today's exchange rate or updates released yesterday. Since the model cannot itself know what happened after it was trained, the app must have a search function. Creating an isolated environment for searching, organizing results, and executing code takes a lot of time and requires constant retouching even after creation.

In this class, we will look at what server tools are, which are executed on behalf of the API provider's server, and how they are different from direct implementation tools, which are executed by your own code. Next, we compare how the three providers provide web search and code execution using the same framework, and at the end, we use examples to confirm the decision order to select the one with less burden of change.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the types and roles of server tools such as web search and code execution
You can decide which has the least burden of change between direct implementation tools and provided tools.

screens.title: Search and code execution: Should I make it myself or use one?
screens.lead: First, read about situations frequently encountered in the app development field. After reading, think about which choice will make you less likely to have to fix it later.

visual.alt: A flowchart that divides the questions into two parts: direct implementation and delivery tools.
labels: In-house Q&A app: What is the exchange rate today?
Direct implementation: I create search linkage, result organization, and code sandbox.
Provided tools: Declare tools in the tools item.
Which one will require less fixing later?

paragraphs: We have a team that runs an in-house question-and-answer app. One day, users started asking for the latest information, such as today's exchange rate or yesterday's update. Because the model itself cannot know what happened after it was trained, the app must have the ability to retrieve information from the web to provide an answer.

There are two paths to a team. One way is to connect the search service API, organize the results so that the model is easy to read, and even build a sandbox to safely execute code for questions that require calculations. This route takes several weeks. The other way is to declare the tools provided by the API provider in the `tools` item of the request. A declaration can start with one line:

If you look at the speed of making it the first time, the second way is faster. But the question this class asks is not about speed but about the burden of change. When search providers change response formats or security needs change, you need to consider who makes the changes and where. Let's answer this question after understanding the difference between server tools and direct implementation tools.

callout.label: question of the day
callout.text: Which one will I end up having to fix later? At the end of class, we organize them in order of judgment.

screens.outro: Let me start by recalling my memory of fixing a tool I made myself.

screens.title: Memories of fixing the tools I made
screens.lead: Have you ever thought about the cost of maintaining the tools you implement? As you select each item, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Who fixed it when the external search service's response format changed?
items.answer: If it's a tool you implement yourself, the person who fixes it is ultimately your team. If an external service changes the field name or response structure, the parsing code will be broken, and the shape of the result returned to the model must be adjusted again. Since these modifications are not about creating new features, but rather about preserving features that already exist, they are less noticeable, but they still take up time.

items.prompt: Who was responsible for security isolation when attaching code execution capabilities?
items.answer: To run the code produced by your model, you must have an isolated environment separate from other systems. If I implement it myself, the isolation design, permission restrictions, and inspection are all up to me. It may seem like a one-time thing to do, but security is not a one-time thing.

items.prompt: If you have ten tools, how many places will you need to check?
items.answer: If you have implemented ten tools, there are ten places to check. This is because each tool has its own calling conventions, error handling, and external service dependencies. As the number of tools increases, the maintenance burden increases in proportion to the number of tools. So this class tells you to look at what's already available before building a tool.

screens.outro: Now that we've woken up to cost awareness, let's check out what server tools actually are.

screens.title: What are server tools: the platform takes over execution
screens.lead: The following steps show how the same question is handled differently in server tools and direct implementation tools. Select the right arrow to go through the steps one by one.

visual.alt: A two-line flowchart comparing who runs the tools in direct implementation tools and server tools.
labels: What my code does: Tool declaration

steps.title: What are server tools?
steps.body: A server tool is a tool in which the API provider's server executes the tool instead. Examples include web browsing and code execution. My code simply declares which tool to use for the request, and the platform is left to actually run the tool.

steps.title: The model determines when to search
steps.body: For example, with Claude's web search tool, after you add the tool to a request, Claude looks at the prompts and decides for himself when to search. Search for information that changes, such as recent news or current prices, or information outside the scope of study. Stable knowledge, such as math or coding concepts, is answered immediately without searching.

steps.title: The platform runs the search
steps.body: Once the search point is determined, the API runs the search and passes the results to Claude. This process can be repeated multiple times within a single request. My code doesn't need a function to call the search or pass the results to the model.

steps.title: Final answer with source
steps.body: At the end of his turn, Claude compiles his search results and gives a final answer with a source. OpenAI turns on web search by setting `web_search` in the `tools` array in the Responses API, and Gemini does the same with Grounding with Google Search by putting `google_search` in `tools`. Even though the provider is different, the declaration structure is the same.

steps.title: Differences from direct implementation tools
steps.body: With a direct implementation tool, when the model requests a call, my code must receive the request, run the tool, and send back the results. Receiving the request, executing it, handling errors, and returning the results are all up to my code. This difference becomes the standard for all subsequent judgments.

screens.outro: Now that we've confirmed the concept, let's compare the server tools from the three providers in the same framework.

screens.title: Viewing the 3rd party server tools in the same framework
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the three providers' web search tools in the same order: how to turn them on, how to search, and how to provide sources.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body:
**How to turn it on**: Declare in the form `tools=[{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search", "max_uses": 5}]`. `max_uses` is the upper limit on the number of searches that can be made in one request.

**How ​​to search**: There are three versions of the tool. `web_search_20250305` is basic web search, `web_search_20260209` adds dynamic filtering. `web_search_20260318` adds the ability to control whether responses are included in agentic flows. Dynamic filtering is a feature where Claude writes code to filter search results before they enter the context, leaving only the content you need.

**Credit Source**: Your response includes citations of sources taken from your search results.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body:
**How to turn it on**: Declare it in the Responses API request in the form `tools=[{"type": "web_search"}]`. If you are newly linking, use this form.

**Search Method**: There are three types: Non-inferential web search, where questions are asked and answers based on search results, agent-type search, where an inference model plans and repeats the search, and deep research, which examines multiple sources in depth. Deep research can take several minutes to complete, so background mode is recommended.

**Source Provided**: Source citations are included in the response body.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body:
**How to turn it on**: Put `google_search` in `tools` like `tools=[{"type": "google_search"}]`. The name of this feature is Grounding with Google Search.

**Retrieval**: Models are connected to real-time web content, so they can answer questions about updates beyond the time they were trained. The model determines whether to search or not by looking at the question.

**Provide Source**: Sources are provided on which web source the answer is based on, so users can check the facts themselves.

tabs.label: common ground
tabs.body:
For all three providers, the tool declaration ends with one entry in the `tools` array. The model decides whether to search or not, and the platform server executes the search.

So there is no function in my code to run the search. This is the biggest difference from direct implementation tools. The format names and options of the three providers are different, so when changing providers, only the declaration part needs to be modified to match the new format.

screens.outro: Now that we've compared searches, let's next look at code execution tools and their cost structures.

screens.title: Code execution tools and cost structure
screens.lead: Switch between the two states below to compare the cost structure for using the code execution tool alone and in conjunction with web search.

visual.alt: Illustration showing commands and file editing being executed inside an isolated sandbox.

states.label: Use with search
states.body:
Claude's code execution tool executes Bash commands and edits files in a secure, isolated sandbox environment. Things like data analysis, visualization, complex calculations, and uploaded file processing can all be done within API conversations.

When used with a web search or web fetch tool, there is no additional charge for executing the code itself, only the standard token cost. This applies to flows such as dynamic filtering, which filters search results through code.

states.label: exclusive use
states.body:
If you use a separate code execution tool, fees for code execution apply separately from the standard token cost. The cost of the same function varies depending on the request configuration, so you should check the combination before turning on the tool.

The versions of the code execution tool are `code_execution_20250825`, `code_execution_20260120`, and `code_execution_20260521`. From `code_execution_20260120`, the REPL state is maintained, so variables created in previous calls can be used continuously.

screens.outro: Now that we know what the tools do, let's explain how server tools intervene in real-world questions.

screens.title: Case Commentary: How Server Tools Intervene in Latest Information Questions
screens.lead: The instructor explains the process of processing one user question in response blocks. Select the right arrow to follow step by step and see who did what.

steps.title: What my code did: declaration
steps.body: A user asked what the new SDK version was released this week. My code just declared one line `web_search` to `tools` in the request. There is no function anywhere to run the search.

steps.title: Response Block 1: server_tool_use
steps.body: The response first appears with a `{"type": "server_tool_use", "name": "web_search"}` block. This is a record that the model determined that this question required a search and created a search term. The one who made the judgment was the model.

steps.title: Response block 2: web_search_tool_result
steps.body: Next comes the `{"type": "web_search_tool_result"}` block. This is the result returned by the platform server executing the search. If necessary, these two types of blocks are repeated multiple times within a request. It's the platform that runs it, not my code.

steps.title: Response Block 3: Text with Source
steps.body: Finally, there is a `text` block, followed by a quote of the form `web_search_result_location`. The model synthesizes the search results and provides an answer with the source. Users will see this text and its source.

steps.title: When the limit is exceeded
steps.body: If the model attempts to retrieve more than `max_uses`, the search results block will contain error code `max_uses_exceeded`. This signal is not a bug for my code to fix, but rather a reminder to decide whether to adjust the `max_uses` value in the declaration.

steps.title: If it were implemented directly
steps.body: If you implemented the same thing yourself, your code would receive the `tool_use` request sent by the model, call the search service, organize the results, and write code that returns `tool_result`. In server tools, all of this is left out and only the declaration remains.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the flow, we will summarize how to judge based on the burden of change.

screens.title: Decide that change is a burden and correct incorrect declarations
screens.lead: The instructor organizes the judgment criteria line by line and corrects one incorrect declaration at the end. Select the right arrow and follow the steps in order.

visual.alt: Illustration comparing the maintenance burden of direct implementation and provided tools on both scales.
labels: Implement it yourself: I manage search provider changes, parsing rules, and sandbox isolation.
Provided tools: Specification changes are customized by the provider
Is it a provided tool? -> If so, start with that -> If not, implement it yourself.

steps.title: As for the provided tools, the provider adapts to specification changes.
steps.body: If you use a provided tool, there is less need to modify your code because the provider adapts when the API specifications change. You only need to manage one item that declares a tool.

steps.title: Direct implementation increases management items
steps.body: If I implement it myself, I have to move it whenever I change search providers, when response parsing rules change, or when I check the isolation of the code execution sandbox. As the number of tools increases, this burden also increases.

steps.title: When direct implementation is advantageous
steps.body: Direct implementation is appropriate when dealing with data that cannot be reached by provided tools, such as an in-house DB. In this case, when the model requests a call, my code executes it and returns the result. Delivery tools are only effective in areas the provider can reach, such as the web.

steps.title: judgment order
steps.body: First, make sure it is a provided tool. Second, when I get to it, I write about it first. Third, only areas that do not work are implemented directly. Depending on the tool, there is a per-call fee, so you'll need to factor in your expected usage as well.

steps.title: Reading incorrect declaration
steps.body: Please read the following declaration: `{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search", "allowed_domains": ["docs.example.com"], "blocked_domains": ["ads.example.com"]}` This declaration contains both a whitelist and a blacklist.

steps.title: Fix declaration
steps.body: `allowed_domains` and `blocked_domains` only use one of the two. Since your search has already been narrowed by the whitelist, delete the line `blocked_domains`. The modified declaration is `{"type": "web_search_20250305", "name": "web_search", "allowed_domains": ["docs.example.com"]}`.

screens.outro: Now that we have summarized the criteria for judgment, let us conclude with the key points.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the key points of this lesson on one screen. Read the paragraph below and proceed to the summary screen.

paragraphs: Server tools are executed by the platform, and direct implementation tools are executed by your code. Web browsing and code execution are available as provisioning tools for all three providers, so let's look at the provisioning tools before building these general-purpose features ourselves.

When choosing a tool, the criterion is the burden of change. As a provision tool, only things that cannot be reached, such as in-house data, are directly implemented. Costs are both tool-specific fees and token costs.

glossary.def: This is a tool in which the API provider's server executes the tool instead. Examples include web browsing and code execution.
It is a tool that when the model requests a call, my code receives it, executes it, and returns the result.
Claude Web Search is a feature that filters search results with code before they enter the context, leaving only the necessary content.
This is a feature where Gemini connects to real-time web content using the google_search tool and provides evidence-based answers.
This is the cost of having to continually fix the tool due to external specification changes and error response.

misconceptions.myth: Server tools always come at no additional cost.
misconceptions.fact: The code execution tool has no additional charges and only costs standard tokens when used with web search or web fetch. Otherwise, separate code execution fees apply.

misconceptions.myth: If you declare a server tool, the model will always search for it.
misconceptions.fact: The model determines whether to search by looking at the request content. Answer questions about stable knowledge directly without searching.

misconceptions.myth: If there is a provided tool, there is no need to implement it yourself.
misconceptions.fact: In areas where provided tools cannot reach, such as in-house DB, direct implementation is required. The standard is to directly implement only what the provided tool can do and only what the provided tool cannot do.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Priority is given to those with lower change burden.
Server tools are executed by the platform, reducing the need to modify my code.
All three providers have the same tools for web browsing and code execution.
The cost is calculated by looking at the fee for each tool and the token cost.
